head: 5654d9b2979db5964482574059927f0595467ba1
summary: This slice fixed a genuine lost-cancel race in SynchronousIoCancel.CancelLoop: the single canceller thread could get stuck inside a blocking CancelSynchronousIo call once the target thread re-blocked, silently killing the 25 ms resend and leaving guarded I/O blocked indefinitely under load. The fix dispatches each cancel attempt on its own short-lived thread (capped at 4 concurrent) and adds a gate-and-drain protocol to Exit/Dispose guaranteeing no stray cancel after the guard is left. It took 3 risk-spike rounds, 2 design rounds, 2 critique rounds and 2 code-review rounds, plus custom kernel-thread tracing, to prove the mechanism actually works. Two minor test-coverage obligations code-review raised (O-026, O-027) were accepted but never built.

candidates.title: Discharge O-026 and O-027 (Dispose-drain and cap-of-4 test-coverage gaps)
candidates.why: Both were accepted-pending at code-review's second pass but never built; they remain open obligations owed to build-slice with no subsequent build-slice run to fix them, and validate-slice ran and passed anyway.

candidates.title: Fix the pre-existing 250 ms Cancel() latency flake exposed under load
candidates.why: Build-slice and validate-slice both found CancelInterruptsACallBlockedInTheKernel, CancellationTests.CancelReturnsFromAScanStuckInItsFirstCall, CancelAtRandomMomentsEndsEveryScanCleanlyAndLeavesNoStrayCancel's calibration, and ScanStoreRollupTimingTests all fail their timing bars under the same loaded conditions this slice's proof protocol uses, in both the fixed and unfixed tree; the design's own open question about whether this is SL-055's or a separate slice was never answered by a person.

candidates.title: Verify CancelSynchronousIo held-in-kernel/reclaim behavior on Windows 10
candidates.why: The fix's two core premises (a second concurrent cancel frees a re-blocked wait; held attempts are reclaimed once target I/O completes) were measured only on Windows 11 26200 and contradict Microsoft's documented Remarks; the project also targets Windows 10, which is untested.

candidates.title: Harden the loaded-test harness against protocol/discovery stalls
candidates.why: Loaded loops hit machine-wide starvation twice during this slice: a 2-minute test-discovery stall with the test thread still in its pre-Cancel Sleep(200), and a 'Failed to negotiate protocol ... 90 seconds' failure; build-slice suggested raising VSTEST_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT and treating no-result runs as infra failures.

candidates.title: Re-tier future SynchronousIoCancel.cs slices to high risk with more than one designer
candidates.why: This slice and SL-024 both needed heavy rework (3 risk-spike rounds, 2 design rounds, 2 critique rounds, 2 code-review rounds here) to get this file's kernel-level concurrency right from a single uncontested design.

candidates.title: Find a way to reproduce the design's actual load shape (32 busy-loop jobs / 16 logical CPUs) at validate
candidates.why: Validate's machine rules cap load at 8 logical CPUs, so it substituted 2-CPU pinned contention instead of the design's specified shape; the substitute discriminates but was never confirmed equivalent to what the design asked for.

payload.estimate_error: Opened as medium size, medium risk, 1 designer, sized by a person. The risk tier was too low: the fix needed 3 risk-spike rounds, 2 design rounds, 2 critique rounds and 2 code-review rounds, plus custom instrumented kernel-thread tracing to settle premises unit tests alone couldn't reach, and it rests on undocumented OS behavior (CancelSynchronousIo held-in-kernel) measured on only one Windows build. A single uncontested designer shipped 4 major findings, one of which (the cap-of-4 rationale) was directly contradicted by evidence already in hand before the design was written. Given this project's own precedent of bumping scanner-adjacent slices to a harder tier (Q-002) and that SL-024 previously hit this exact file with similar difficulty, work in SynchronousIoCancel.cs should default to high risk with more than one designer, not medium.

learned.lesson: Any change to SynchronousIoCancel.cs should be tiered high risk by default, not medium.
learned.evidence: This one file needed 3 risk-spike rounds, 2 design rounds, 2 critique rounds and 2 code-review rounds to land a fix; SL-024 previously hit the same file with a comparable signature (1 attempt made, 0 delivered, canceller blocked).

learned.lesson: The validate machine caps load at half its logical CPUs (8 of 16); a design's load-based proof protocol must be checked against that cap, not against what a risk-spike's own scratch environment could run.
learned.evidence: validate-slice: 'the machine rules limit load to half the logical CPUs, so the design's 32 busy jobs were not allowed ... 8 unpinned busy loops did not reproduce the flake on the unfixed guard', forcing a pinned-2-CPU substitute.

learned.lesson: .taad/fitness.yaml already permits ThreadPool.UnsafeQueueUserWorkItem inside SynchronousIoCancel.cs's Close method; any new rule banning ThreadPool/Timer patterns in that file must exempt that call by name or it breaks on existing, correct code.
learned.evidence: m3/m7 findings: rule 2's `\bThreadPool\b` fired on the existing Close hand-off at SynchronousIoCancel.cs:168, requiring the fix `\bThreadPool\.(?!UnsafeQueueUserWorkItem\b)`.

learned.lesson: In this engine, a design's architecture_rules are appended to .taad/fitness.yaml automatically as soon as design runs, before critique sees it; a stage that trusts an earlier survey's git snapshot as current is already stale.
learned.evidence: m7: the survey recorded no tracked file modified, but by critique time fitness.yaml already showed both new rules appended at lines 606-626.

learned.lesson: A design's numeric rationale for a bound (retry cap, attempt count, etc.) must be checked against the failing test's own captured output before it is finalized, not against theory alone.
learned.evidence: M3: the design justified a cap of 4 with 'in theory 2 suffice, since each new attempt frees the one waiting on the I/O it cancels', but the repro's own captured failure ('interrupted 1 time(s), 1 cancel attempt(s) made') already showed the held attempt was not waiting on the wait it cancelled.

learned.lesson: accepted-pending obligations from a second code-review round do not automatically force another build-slice pass in this engine; validate-slice can run and pass while such obligations stand open.
learned.evidence: code-review's second pass filed m1/m2 as accepted-pending (O-026, O-027), but no build-slice #2 appears in the stage history, and validate-slice #1 still passed.

learned.lesson: The fix's core premises (a second concurrent CancelSynchronousIo frees a re-blocked wait; a held call is reclaimed once target I/O completes) were measured only on Windows 11 26200 and contradict Microsoft's documented Remarks, and this project also ships on Windows 10.
learned.evidence: validate-slice: 'not reached: Windows 10 was not tested ... measured only on Windows 11 26200'; m5 quoting Microsoft's contradictory Remarks.

missed.what: The design's proof protocol specified 32 busy-loop jobs on 16 logical CPUs as the load for proving the fix, without checking whether the environment that would run it could actually sustain that load. Critique reviewed the protocol's filter coverage (M1) and idle-vs-loaded distinction (m6) in fine detail but never questioned the load shape's feasibility.
missed.caught_by: validate-slice, which found machine rules cap load at 8 logical CPUs and had to substitute confined 2-CPU pinned contention instead of the design's specified shape.

missed.what: Critique required a hang-timeout and dump (m4) for the guard's own drain hanging, but did not anticipate that the loaded test runner itself could stall on test discovery or VSTest protocol negotiation, unrelated to the guard.
missed.caught_by: build-slice's loaded loops, which hit a 2-minute discovery stall (test thread still in its pre-Cancel Sleep(200)) and a 90-second protocol-negotiation failure, both manually classified as infra failures.

payload.reason: Two fix obligations from code-review's second pass (O-026, O-027) remain open, owed to build-slice, and were never discharged by a subsequent build-slice run before validate-slice ran and passed. Per this project's own rule, the gate they are aimed at cannot be considered to have passed cleanly while they stand, so this slice is not clean to commit as-is.

It took 3 risk-spike rounds, 2 design rounds, 2 critique rounds and 2 code-review rounds, plus custom kernel-thread tracing, to prove the mechanism actually works. unknowns: Does CancelSynchronousIo exhibit the same held-in-kernel-until-target-completes behavior on Windows 10, or only on the Windows 11 26200 build this was measured on?
Is the pre-existing 250 ms 'Cancel() took N ms' timing-bar failure under load its own defect needing a separate slice, or an accepted limitation? The design raised this and no person has answered it.
Does the acceptance repro's 2 s bar have enough margin under real contention on other machines, given it reached 1780-2051 ms under validate's pinned-2-CPU load?
Will validate's load cap ever be raised (or worked around) so the design's actual specified load shape (32 jobs / 16 CPUs) can be run directly instead of substituted?
what_went_wrong: risk-spike ran 3 times: round 1 halted with no experiment deciding anything; round 2 halted with 1 held and 2 no-go verdicts; round 3 proceeded to design despite the standing no-go on 'retry-cancel-loop-clears-flake-without-collateral', with a model treating the untested premise as a working assumption (O-005) instead of spiking it directly.

design-slice ran twice: round 1 halted on 2 questions that are still open on the project's list today; round 2 was accepted by a model while the project owner was away, so this design never got the owner's actual sign-off.

A single, uncontested design shipped 4 major and 7 minor findings at critique, including a cap-of-4 rationale ('in theory 2 suffice') directly contradicted by the failing test's own captured output that was available before the design was written (M3).

code-review's second pass found 2 more test-coverage gaps (C-008's Dispose test never has an attempt in flight; C-010's cap test never asserts the peak) after critique had already passed the design; these were accepted-pending as O-026/O-027 but no build-slice re-run ever fixed them, and the slice proceeded through validate-slice regardless.

The design's proof protocol specified a load shape (32 busy-loop jobs on 16 logical CPUs) that validate's own machine rules disallow (capped at 8), discovered only when validate tried to run it; validate substituted differently-shaped contention (2 pinned CPUs) that discriminates but was never the design's own tested shape.

Loaded test runs hit two unrelated infrastructure stalls (a 2-minute test-discovery hang and a 90-second VSTest protocol-negotiation failure) that had to be manually classified as infra failures rather than real results.
